generator.params.apical.why: A fir, spruce, hemlock or Douglas-fir holds its branches under its leader (apical control): each year a branch grows about half as far as the leader rises, so the crown is a cone about as wide as its depth, and stays pointed as the leader slows.

generator.params.bend_set.why: The family's limbs spring back from most of each year's sag: Farjon gives its branches as horizontal or spreading, the lower ones curving down only at their ends. Keeping half of each year's sag, a limb grown 150 years hung flat against the trunk and the old crown stood as a column.

generator.params.side_order.why: An old fir, spruce, hemlock or Douglas-fir keeps its limbs leafy by branching them again and again: second-order shoots set twigs of their own, so a limb ends in a dense fan of foliage. Branching only once, every old crown was a fishbone of bare whips with needles at their tips.

generator.params.twig_years.why: The twigs on a limb's side shoots live about as long as their needles and are replaced from below; kept for ever, the fully branched crown passed the program's module limit before 200 years.

generator.params.epi_years.why: A limb's dormant buds wait as long as the limb lives and resprout it where light reaches them: old Douglas-fir crowns keep their foliage by such epicormic shoots (Ishii & Ford 2001), as old firs, spruces and hemlocks reiterate theirs. Living 80 years, the buds were spent before the crown aged, and old crowns lost three quarters of their foliage between 150 and 300 years.

generator.params.epi_order.why: The dormant buds that resprout an old limb wait along its main axis, where its epicormic shoots stand (Ishii & Ford 2001); buds kept on every side shoot as well filled the program's module limit before 300 years.

generator.params.branch_floor.why: Once the leader slows, a lit limb still lengthens a few centimetres a year, so the old crown keeps its spread instead of stopping where the leader did.

generator.params.apical_light.why: Shade strengthens apical control: a shaded branch takes a smaller share of the leader's shoot than a lit one, so a tree grown in a stand keeps a narrow crown while its leader races up (forest-grown Douglas-fir about 3 m across its crown at 30 years, its trunk about 25 cm through). Taking the full share in any light, the shaded limbs of a stand-grown Douglas-fir spread 4 m and carried four times the needles, and its trunk grew twice as thick as stand-grown trees'.

generator.params.side_floor.why: Once the leader stops rising, a limb's side shoots still grow a few centimetres a year and set twigs, renewing the foliage along it. Held to the leader's dwindling growth with the limb's own tip, they shrank to millimetres and set almost no twigs, and old crowns lost their foliage after 150 years (grand fir, Douglas-fir, western hemlock).

generator.params.floor_ramp.why: The side shoots' floor comes in over the top 10 m of an old tree, so its top stays narrow: in full to the treetop, the short limbs of an old tree's top whorls carried side shoots longer than themselves, and the tops of 300-year Douglas-fir, Sitka spruce and subalpine fir were domes two to four times as wide as photographed ones (inaturalist-crowns-2026-10: the top tenth .06 to .12 of the height).

generator.params.limb_light.why: An old limb is shed for want of light only when its tips catch little light for the wood they carry, a third as readily as the pines' 0.01: a fully branched old limb carries many segments, and at 0.01 limbs whose foliage was well lit were shed for their size, so subalpine fir and western larch lost four fifths of their foliage between 150 and 300 years.

generator.params.limb_tip.why: A limb older than limb_age whose tips' mean light has fallen to the starving point is shed whatever its size, as a shaded limb dies once its foliage no longer pays for it (branch autonomy): with the per-segment rule eased, shaded limbs would otherwise linger and fill the program's module limit.

generator.params.seg_min.why: An old limb's slow shoots, a centimetre or two a year, are laid down as one shoot every few years with the same needle area, so a fully branched old crown keeps its side shoots within the program's module and segment limits: laid down every year, old Douglas-fir and western hemlock passed them unless their inner side shoots were shed or cut short (side_years), which left their lower limbs bare whips. Young shoots, longer than 8 cm a year, grow as before.

generator.params.bud_length.why: A shoot shorter than 10 cm sets proportionally fewer side buds, so a slow old crown no longer smothers itself in buds (pinidae revision 13); set for the family, as the yews and cypresses it was not fitted on branch as before.

generator.params.top_ramp.why: Branch shoots are shortest in the top whorls and lengthen over the first metres below the treetop (Cannell et al. 1976, Sitka spruce), so the top is a point: at full length from the first year, young treetops were three to five times as wide as photographed ones.

generator.params.ring_share.why: Once the leader passes half its full height, each square metre of foliage lays down less trunk wood, as (half the full height / height) squared, as taller trees grow less stem for their leaf area (Ryan and Yoder 1997, hydraulic limitation): with the same ring area per leaf at every height, 300-year open-grown trees drew trunks two to three times the floras' (Douglas-fir 5.2 m against Abrams' 1 to 3.5 m and FEIS's 1.5 to 1.8 m common in old growth; grand fir 3.0 m against 1 to 1.5 m, up to 2). Tried at 0.45 and 0.6, 300-year Douglas-fir drew 3.1 and 3.8 m, grand fir 1.7 and 2.1 m, Sitka spruce 2.1 and 2.7 m (to 5 m, Abrams), and the 60-year sizes stayed within 4% of before; 0.5 is between them.

rules.note: Old conifers (pinidae revision 13): apical control as Wilson (2000) describes it, the leader holding its branches' growth below its own. A branch's yearly shoot is a share of the leader's, so a whorl's branches lengthen as the leader above them rises and the crown is a cone. With a fixed yearly length instead, the crowns stood as tubes whose top halves were twice as wide as photographed open-grown trees' (inaturalist-crowns-2026-10); 0.5 is the middle of the six species fitted to those photographs, 0.36 to 0.6. bend_set 0.15 (the same revision): at the Pinidae's 0.5, grand fir and western hemlock grown 150 years carried their limbs hanging against the trunk; at 0.15 grand fir's old crown stays conical. Ramifying old crowns (the same revision): side_order 2 with twigs that live twig_years 10 and dormant buds that live epi_years 80 keep old limbs leafy, as Strieby's (2017) Sitka spruce plate and the old trees photographed show, within the module limit to 300 years (twigs carry one spray of the three's area). branch_floor 0.06 and top_ramp 2 (Cannell et al. 1976) fitted with each species' apical and branch_reach to the same photographs at 15, 60, 150 and 300 years.

traits.note: Abrams (vol. 1, 1923, p. 52), Pinaceae: resinous trees whose linear or needle-like leaves are set in spirals; pollen and seed cones on the same tree; the seed cone woody, ripening in its first or second season.

traits.phyllotaxis_pattern.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 150, family Pinaceae: phyllotaxis pattern spiral; read as "spiral".

traits.leaf_division.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 150, family Pinaceae: leaf division simple; read as "simple".

traits.leaf_habit.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 150, family Pinaceae: leaf habit evergreen (deciduous in Larix and Pseudolarix), usually. Read together as {"evergreen": "usually", "deciduous": "rarely"}.

traits.reproduction.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 151, 152, 153, family Pinaceae: reproduction cones; read as "cones".
